questions.q: Explain React's model (UI = f(state)): what a render is, what triggers one, and how that differs from Angular's change detection.
questions.a:
### Model
A component is a function of props and state returning a description of UI (React elements). React calls it (**render**), compares the result with the previous one (**reconciliation**) and applies the minimal DOM changes (**commit**).

### What triggers a render
- State update in the component ({{setState}} from useState or dispatch from useReducer).
- Parent re-renders (children re-render by default, unless memoised and props unchanged).
- Context value change for consumers.
- External store change via {{useSyncExternalStore}}.
Props changing alone doesn't cause a render; the parent rendering does.

### Render is not commit
Rendering must be **pure** (no side effects): React may render several times, discard renders (concurrent features, StrictMode double-invocation in development), and only commit some. Side effects belong in event handlers or effects.

### vs Angular
| React | Angular |
|---|---|
| re-runs component functions, diffs virtual DOM | compiled templates check bindings; signals mark precise consumers |
| library: choose router, data, forms | framework with built-ins |
| explicit immutability for change detection | signals or OnPush with immutability |
| hooks for state and effects | DI services, signals, RxJS |
Both converge on fine-grained, compiler-assisted rendering (React Compiler, Angular signals).

  R --> D[Diff against previous tree]
  D --> C[Commit phase: apply DOM changes]
  C --> L[useLayoutEffect, then paint]
  L --> E[useEffect after paint]
pts: Render computes UI; commit applies DOM changes.
State updates, parent renders, context, external stores trigger renders.
Renders must be pure; React may discard them.
Derive values during render instead of storing them.
React re-runs functions; Angular checks compiled bindings.

questions.q: How do JSX, props and composition work in React? Show how composition (children, render props, slots) beats configuration-heavy components.
questions.a:
### JSX
Syntax for {{React.createElement}} calls (or the JSX runtime): expressions in braces, attributes as props ({{className}}, {{htmlFor}}), components capitalised. JSX escapes values by default.

### Props
Read-only inputs; one-way data flow from parent to child; callbacks passed down to communicate up. Props should be serialisable-ish data and functions; avoid passing huge objects that change identity every render (affects memoisation).

### Composition patterns
| Pattern | Use |
|---|---|
| {{children}} | wrapper components (Card, Dialog, Layout) |
| named slot props ({{header}}, {{actions}} as ReactNode) | multiple insertion points |
| render props / function children | caller controls rendering with data from the component (list row rendering) |
| compound components (Tabs, Tabs.List, Tabs.Panel with context) | flexible structured UIs |
| custom hooks | share logic without UI |

### Why composition wins
A {{Table}} with 40 boolean props for every variant is hard to use and maintain; a table that accepts column definitions and cell renderers, or compound children, lets teams compose variants without changing the component.
pts: JSX compiles to element creation; escapes by default.
Props are read-only; one-way data flow.
children, slot props, render props, compound components.
Custom hooks share logic.
Composition beats configuration props.

questions.q: Explain reconciliation, the virtual DOM and Fiber. Why are some updates interruptible, and what does that mean for your code?
questions.a:
### Reconciliation
After a render, React compares the new element tree with the previous one using heuristics:
- Different element **type** at the same position: unmount old subtree, mount new.
- Same type: update props, recurse into children.
- Lists: **keys** identify items across renders.
This makes diffing O(n) instead of a general tree diff.

### Virtual DOM
The element tree is a lightweight description; React computes changes and applies them to the real DOM in the commit phase. The point isn't that DOM is slow; it's declarative updates with batching.

### Fiber
React's internal architecture represents work as units (fibers) that can be **paused, resumed, prioritised or discarded**. This enables concurrent rendering: urgent updates (typing) interrupt non-urgent renders (filtering a big list via transitions).

### Implications for code
- Render functions must be pure and idempotent (they may run more than once or be abandoned).
- Don't rely on render order for side effects.
- Changing a component's type or position (conditional wrappers) resets its state.
- Defining components inside other components creates a new type each render: state is lost and performance suffers.

  Y -->|yes, concurrent render| P[Pause, handle urgent input, resume or restart]
  Y -->|no| N[Next fiber]
  N --> W
  P --> W
  W -->|tree complete| CM[Commit: synchronous, never interrupted]
pts: Diff by type and position; keys for lists.
Virtual DOM enables declarative batched updates.

questions.q: Why do keys matter in React lists? What happens with index keys or unstable keys, and how can keys intentionally reset state?
questions.a:
### Purpose
Keys identify list items across renders so React can match old and new elements: preserve DOM nodes and component state for the same item, move them when order changes.

### Index keys
Fine only for static lists that never reorder, insert or filter. Otherwise state and DOM attach to positions, not items: an expanded row, a typed input or a checkbox appears on the wrong item after sorting or deletion.

### Unstable keys
a random key (Math.random()) or keys generated during render: every render remounts every item: lost state, focus loss, poor performance.

### Use
Stable unique ids from data ({{payment.id}}). If items lack ids, generate them once when data is created, not during render.

### Intentional reset
Changing a component's key remounts it with fresh state: {{<PaymentForm key={accountId} />}} resets the form when the user switches accounts, simpler than syncing state with effects.

Index keys break dynamic lists.
Random keys remount everything.
Use stable data ids.
Change keys to reset component state deliberately.

questions.q: Explain useState and useReducer, functional updates, batching, and the rules of hooks. When do you prefer a reducer?
questions.a:
### useState
Holds a value per component instance; the setter schedules a re-render. State updates are **asynchronous and batched** (React 18+ batches inside events, timeouts, promises). Reading state right after setting it gives the old value in the current render.

### Functional updates
{{setCount(c => c + 1)}} uses the latest state; needed when updates depend on previous state, especially multiple updates in one handler or in async callbacks.

### useReducer
State plus a reducer {{(state, action) => newState}}: centralises transitions, easier testing, good for complex state with related fields (wizard steps, form status), and explicit actions for auditability.

### Rules of hooks
1. Call hooks only at the top level (not in loops, conditions, nested functions).
2. Call hooks only from React function components or custom hooks.
React relies on call order to associate hook state; the ESLint plugin enforces it.

### Immutability
Never mutate state objects; create new ones ({{setItems(list => [...list, item])}}) so React detects changes.
pts: State updates are batched and asynchronous.
Functional updates for previous-state dependencies.
useReducer for complex related state and explicit transitions.
Rules of hooks: top level, React functions only.
Immutable updates.
questions.ex: A transfer screen used five useState flags (isEditing, isConfirming, isSubmitting...) that could contradict each other; a race let users submit twice. A reducer with a discriminated union made impossible states unrepresentable and ignored duplicate submits.

questions.q: Explain useEffect semantics (when it runs, dependencies, cleanup), stale closures, and the race condition when fetching in effects.
questions.a:
### Semantics
- Runs **after commit** (after the browser paints, usually); synchronises the component with an external system.
- Dependency array: runs when any dependency changes ({{Object.is}} comparison); empty array runs on mount; no array runs after every render.
- Cleanup runs before the next effect run and on unmount.
- StrictMode in development mounts, unmounts and remounts to surface missing cleanups.

### Stale closures
Effects and callbacks capture values from the render in which they were created. An interval reading {{count}} without listing it as a dependency always sees the initial value. Fix: include dependencies (lint rule exhaustive-deps), use functional updates, or refs for latest values.

### Fetch race condition
User switches account A to B quickly; A's response arrives after B's and overwrites it. Fix: cleanup with an ignore flag or AbortController; better, use a data library (TanStack Query) or framework loaders.

### Effects are for external systems
Subscriptions, timers, DOM APIs, non-React widgets. Not for deriving state or handling user events (q16).

questions.q: When do React.memo, useMemo and useCallback actually help? What does the React Compiler change?
questions.a:
### What they do
- {{React.memo(Component)}}: skip re-rendering if props are shallowly equal.
- {{useMemo(fn, deps)}}: cache a computed value between renders.
- {{useCallback(fn, deps)}}: cache a function identity.

### When they help
- Expensive renders of components whose props rarely change (large lists, charts) wrapped in memo, **and** parents pass stable props (memoised callbacks and objects).
- Expensive computations (filtering 10,000 rows) with useMemo.
- Stable identities required by dependency arrays or memoised children.

### When they don't
- Cheap components: memo comparison costs more than rendering.
- Props that change every render anyway (inline objects, new arrays): memo never hits.
- Premature use everywhere adds noise and bugs (stale dependencies).

### React Compiler
A build-time compiler (stable in 2025) that **automatically memoises** components and hooks, inserting the equivalent of memo, useMemo and useCallback where safe, based on analysing data flow. It requires code to follow the Rules of React (pure render, immutability). With it, manual memoisation is rarely needed; profiling still guides remaining hotspots.
pts: memo skips renders when props are shallowly equal.
useMemo caches values; useCallback caches functions.
Help only with expensive renders and stable props.
Overuse adds cost and bugs.
React Compiler auto-memoises code following the Rules of React.

questions.q: What is React Context good for, why does it cause re-render problems, and how do you structure it?
questions.a:
### Good for
Dependency injection of rarely-changing values: theme, locale, authenticated user summary, feature flags, service clients, compound component internal state.

### Problem
Every consumer re-renders when the context **value identity** changes. Putting frequently changing state (form values, live prices, a big object recreated each render) in a single context re-renders the whole subtree of consumers.

### Structuring
- **Split contexts** by change frequency and concern (UserContext, ThemeContext, separate state and dispatch contexts).
- **Memoise the value** ({{useMemo}}) so identity changes only when content changes.
- Provide **dispatch separately** from state so components that only dispatch don't re-render.
- For high-frequency or large shared state, use a store with **selectors** (Zustand, Redux Toolkit, Jotai) via {{useSyncExternalStore}} so components subscribe to slices.
- Keep providers as low in the tree as possible.

### React 19
{{use(Context)}} can be called conditionally; context as provider ({{<ThemeContext value=...>}}).
pts: Context for rarely changing shared values.
Consumers re-render on value identity change.
Split contexts; memoise values; separate dispatch.
Stores with selectors for high-frequency state.
React 19: use() and context as provider.

questions.q: How do you design good custom hooks? Show a reusable hook for a banking concern and explain common mistakes.
questions.a:
### Principles
- A custom hook **extracts stateful logic** (not UI) for reuse: it composes other hooks and returns values and functions.
- Name with {{use}} prefix; follow rules of hooks.
- Clear inputs and outputs; return objects for multiple values (named) or tuples for state-like pairs.
- Hide implementation details (fetching library, subscriptions) behind a domain-oriented API ({{useAccount(id)}}, not {{useFetch('/accounts/...')}} everywhere).
- Handle cleanup inside the hook.
- Keep hooks focused; compose rather than build mega-hooks.

### Common mistakes
| Mistake | Problem |
|---|---|
| hooks that return new objects every render | breaks memoisation of consumers |
| hiding effects that sync derived state | extra renders, bugs |
| sharing state assumptions (each call has its own state) | developers expect singletons |
| generic mega hooks with many flags | hard to understand |
| missing cancellation | races |
pts: Hooks extract stateful logic, not UI.
Domain-oriented APIs hide implementation.
Cleanup inside the hook; refs for latest callbacks.
Each call has its own state.
Stable return values; focused hooks.

questions.q: Why separate server state from client state? Explain TanStack Query's model (query keys, staleTime, cache invalidation, mutations) for a banking app.
questions.a:
### Server state is different
It's owned by the server, shared across components, can become stale, needs caching, deduplication, background refresh, retries and invalidation. Putting it in Redux or component state reinvents all of that badly.

### TanStack Query model
- **Query keys** identify data ({{['accounts', customerId]}}, {{['transactions', accountId, { month }]}}); identical keys dedupe requests and share cache.
- **staleTime**: how long data is considered fresh (no refetch); **gcTime**: how long unused data stays cached.
- Refetch on window focus, reconnect, interval (configurable; often off or tuned for banking).
- **Mutations** with {{onSuccess}} invalidating related queries ({{queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['accounts'] })}}) or updating cache directly.
- Suspense support, prefetching, pagination and infinite queries.

### Banking choices
- Balances: short staleTime, refetch after payments (invalidate), not optimistic.
- Reference data (payees, branches): longer staleTime.
- Clear the cache on logout (no data leakage between sessions).
- Errors surfaced with retry limits; no retries on 4xx.

  QC -->|stale| BG[Return cached data and refetch in background]
  QC -->|missing| F[Fetch, show loading]
  M[Mutation: make payment] -->|on success| INV[Invalidate accounts and transactions keys]
  INV --> QC
pts: Server state needs caching, dedupe, refresh, invalidation.
Query keys identify and share data.
staleTime and gcTime control freshness and retention.

questions.q: For client state, compare useState/useReducer plus context, Redux Toolkit, and Zustand. How do you choose for a large banking app?
questions.a:
### First, classify state
| Kind | Where |
|---|---|
| Server state (accounts, transactions) | TanStack Query or framework loaders |
| URL state (filters, tabs, pagination) | the router (search params): shareable, back-button friendly |
| Form state | form library or local state |
| Local UI state | useState / useReducer |
| Shared client state (wizard progress, selected account, UI preferences, live market data) | context (rarely changing) or a store |

### Stores
| Option | Strengths | Costs |
|---|---|---|
| **Redux Toolkit** | predictable actions and reducers, devtools time travel, middleware, RTK Query, strong conventions for large teams | more ceremony |
| **Zustand** | tiny, hooks with selectors, minimal boilerplate, works outside React | fewer conventions; teams must agree patterns |
| Jotai or similar | atomic state, fine-grained | different mental model |

### Choosing
Most apps need little global client state once server and URL state are handled properly. Choose Redux Toolkit when many teams need strict conventions and auditability of state changes; Zustand for lightweight shared state with selectors; avoid putting everything into a global store.

questions.q: Build a payment form in React: React Hook Form with Zod validation vs React 19 actions (useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic). When do you use which?
questions.a:
### React Hook Form + Zod
- Uncontrolled inputs by default (fewer renders), schema validation shared with the server if using TypeScript end to end, field-level errors, dynamic field arrays, great for complex client-side forms.

### React 19 actions
- {{<form action={fn}>}} with async functions; {{useActionState}} returns state and pending; {{useFormStatus}} for submit buttons; {{useOptimistic}} for optimistic UI.
- Works with server functions in frameworks (Next.js server actions), progressive enhancement.

### Choosing
| Need | Choice |
|---|---|
| complex client validation, dynamic fields, wizards | React Hook Form + Zod |
| simple forms, server-centric (RSC frameworks), progressive enhancement | actions |
| both | actions for submission with RHF for client validation |

### Banking specifics
- Server validation remains authoritative (Zod on the client is UX).
- Prevent double submission (pending state disables button; idempotency key per payment intent).
- **No optimistic UI for money movement outcomes**: show "pending" until the server confirms.
- Accessible errors (aria-invalid, aria-describedby, error summary).
pts: RHF + Zod for complex client forms.
React 19 actions for simple and server-centric forms.
Server validation authoritative.
Pending state plus idempotency key against double submits.
No optimistic outcomes for money movement.

questions.q: Explain error boundaries and Suspense. How do you design loading and error states for a dashboard so one failing widget doesn't break the page?
questions.a:
### Error boundaries
Catch rendering errors in their subtree and render a fallback. They don't catch errors in event handlers, async code outside rendering, or server errors unless rethrown during render (data libraries can throw to boundaries). Class components or libraries ({{react-error-boundary}}) implement them.

### Suspense
Declarative loading: a component that suspends (lazy component, data via {{use(promise)}} or Suspense-enabled libraries) shows the nearest {{<Suspense fallback>}} until ready. Nested boundaries control granularity; transitions keep showing old content instead of fallbacks during updates.

### Dashboard design
- Wrap each widget in its own error boundary and Suspense boundary: independent failure and loading.
- Critical data (balances) at the top with careful fallback; non-critical widgets (offers, insights) degrade silently with "unavailable" messages.
- Reset boundaries on retry or when keys change (resetKeys).
- Report errors to telemetry in onError.
- Skeletons sized to final content to avoid layout shift.

  EB3 --> S3[Suspense] --> O[Offers widget]

questions.q: Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs, refs, and imperative handles: when do you need each? What changed with refs in React 19?
questions.a:
### Controlled inputs
Value held in React state, updated via onChange: single source of truth, immediate validation and formatting, but a render per keystroke (fine for most forms).

### Uncontrolled inputs
DOM holds the value; read via refs or form submission (FormData): fewer renders, good for large forms (React Hook Form uses this).

### Refs
{{useRef}} holds mutable values that don't trigger renders: DOM nodes (focus, measure, scroll), timers, latest callbacks, previous values. Reading or writing refs during render breaks purity (except lazy initialisation).

### Imperative handles
{{useImperativeHandle}} exposes a limited API from a child (focus, reset) instead of the raw DOM node, for design-system components.

### React 19 changes
- {{ref}} is a regular prop for function components: {{forwardRef}} is no longer needed.
- Ref callbacks can return a cleanup function.

### Guidance
Prefer declarative props; use refs for DOM integration and imperative edges (focus management, third-party widgets).

Uncontrolled: DOM-held, fewer renders.
Refs for DOM and mutable values; not during render.
useImperativeHandle for limited APIs.
React 19: ref as prop; ref callback cleanup.

questions.q: Design routing for a React banking app: route-based code splitting, data loading (loaders vs component fetching), protected routes and URL state.
questions.a:
### Router choices
React Router (v7, with framework mode or library mode) or TanStack Router (type-safe routes and search params). Frameworks (Next.js, React Router framework mode) add file-based routing and server rendering.

### Code splitting
{{React.lazy(() => import(...))}} per route with Suspense; prefetch likely next routes on hover or idle.

### Data loading
- **Loaders** (route-level) start fetching in parallel with code loading and avoid waterfalls (component renders, then fetches, then child fetches).
- Combine loaders with TanStack Query ({{queryClient.ensureQueryData}}) for caching.
- Component-level fetching is fine for independent widgets.

### Protected routes
Route guards redirect unauthenticated users (UX). **Authorisation is enforced by the APIs**; never rely on route protection for security.

### URL state
Filters, tabs, pagination and selected ids in search params: shareable links, back button works, refresh-safe. Type-safe parsing (TanStack Router or Zod).
pts: Lazy routes with Suspense; prefetch next routes.
Loaders fetch in parallel with code, avoiding waterfalls.
Combine loaders with a query cache.
Route protection is UX; APIs authorise.
Filters and pagination in the URL.

questions.q: "You might not need an effect": list the effect anti-patterns and their correct replacements.
questions.a:
| Anti-pattern | Replace with |
|---|---|
| deriving state from props or state in an effect ({{setFullName(first + last)}}) | compute during render |
| expensive derivation in effect + state | {{useMemo}} (or rely on React Compiler) |
| resetting state when a prop changes via effect | change the component **key** |
| adjusting part of state on prop change | store previous value and adjust during render, or restructure state |
| handling user events in effects (submit when flag set) | do it in the event handler |
| sending analytics for user actions in effects | event handlers (effects only for "component was displayed") |
| chains of effects updating each other | a single event handler or reducer computing all next state |
| notifying parent of state changes via effect | update parent state in the same event handler, or lift state up |
| fetching data with manual effects everywhere | data library or framework loaders |
| subscribing to external stores manually | {{useSyncExternalStore}} |

### Legitimate effects
Synchronising with external systems: subscriptions, timers, DOM APIs, third-party widgets, network connections, document title, analytics page views.

### Why it matters
Effects run after paint (extra render, flicker), are easy to get wrong (dependencies, races), and make data flow hard to follow.

Reset state with keys.
Event logic in event handlers.
No effect chains; reducers for multi-field updates.

questions.q: How do you test React components effectively with Testing Library, Vitest and MSW? What should you avoid testing?
questions.a:
### Approach
Test behaviour the user sees: render, interact by role and label, assert visible results. Testing Library encourages accessible queries ({{getByRole}}, {{getByLabelText}}).

### Tooling
| Tool | Use |
|---|---|
| Vitest or Jest | runner |
| React Testing Library + user-event | rendering and realistic interactions |
| **MSW** (Mock Service Worker) | intercept fetch at the network level for deterministic API responses (also in Storybook and dev) |

questions.q: Explain concurrent rendering: startTransition/useTransition and useDeferredValue. Fix a search-as-you-type over 20,000 transactions that freezes typing.
questions.a:
### Problem
Each keystroke filters and renders 20,000 rows synchronously; typing waits for rendering, so input lags (poor INP).

### Concurrent features
- **Transitions** mark updates as non-urgent: React can interrupt them to handle urgent updates (keystrokes), and keeps showing old UI instead of Suspense fallbacks. {{useTransition}} returns {{isPending}}.
- **useDeferredValue** gives a lagging copy of a value: the input updates immediately; the expensive list renders with the deferred value when React has time.

### Fix
1. Input state updates urgently (controlled input stays responsive).
2. Filtering and the list use {{useDeferredValue(query)}}.
3. Memoise the list component so it only re-renders when the deferred value changes.
4. Show a subtle pending indicator when {{query !== deferredQuery}}.
5. **Virtualise** the list (only visible rows rendered): concurrency helps responsiveness, virtualisation reduces work.

### Limits
Concurrent rendering doesn't make work faster; it schedules it better. Heavy computations still need memoisation, virtualisation or web workers.

  R->>R: start rendering 5000 filtered rows
  U->>R: next keystroke
  R->>R: abandon stale transition render, restart with newest value
  R-->>U: list commits when ready, isPending shows a spinner meanwhile

questions.q: What is tearing in concurrent React, and how does useSyncExternalStore prevent it? Write a subscription to an external real-time price store.
questions.a:
### Tearing
With concurrent rendering, React may pause rendering midway; if an external mutable store (not React state) changes during that pause, different components in the same render can read different values: the UI shows inconsistent data (one price in the header, another in the grid).

### useSyncExternalStore
{{useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot?)}}:
- React subscribes to the store and reads snapshots consistently; if the store changes during a concurrent render, React re-renders synchronously to keep the UI consistent.
- {{getSnapshot}} must return a **cached, immutable** value (same reference if unchanged), otherwise infinite re-renders.
- Selectors derive slices; libraries (Zustand, Redux, Jotai) use it internally.

### When you need it
Integrating non-React sources: WebSocket price feeds, browser APIs (online status, media queries), third-party SDK state, cross-framework stores (micro-frontends).

useSyncExternalStore keeps reads consistent.

Selectors for slices.

questions.q: Build a real-time trading blotter in React with thousands of rows and frequent price ticks. What architecture keeps it smooth?
questions.a:
### Architecture
1. **Feed handling off the main thread**: WebSocket in a web worker parses and coalesces ticks (latest per symbol).
2. **External store** (Zustand or custom with useSyncExternalStore) keyed by symbol; ticks applied in batches per animation frame.
3. **Fine-grained subscriptions**: each row or cell subscribes to its own symbol via a selector, so a tick re-renders only that row.
4. **Virtualisation**: only visible rows mounted.
5. **Stable row identities**: keys by trade or symbol id; row components memoised.
6. **Throttled display**: humans can't read 50 updates per second per cell; 4 to 10 visual updates per second is enough; flashing via CSS classes.
7. **Interaction priority**: sorting and filtering in transitions; user input stays urgent.

### Alternatives
For very large grids, a dedicated grid (AG Grid) with its own row-level update APIs, used via React wrappers, bypasses React reconciliation for cell updates.

### Correctness
Prices shown with timestamps and staleness indicators; trading actions validate against server prices, never client-displayed ones.

questions.q: Explain React SSR, hydration and streaming SSR with Suspense. What causes hydration mismatches and how do you avoid them in a banking site?
questions.a:
### SSR and hydration
Server renders HTML (fast first paint, SEO); the client downloads JavaScript and **hydrates**: attaches event handlers and state to existing DOM, expecting the client's first render to match the server's HTML exactly.

### Streaming SSR
{{renderToPipeableStream}} or framework equivalents stream HTML as Suspense boundaries resolve: the shell arrives quickly, slow sections stream in later; **selective hydration** prioritises hydrating the parts users interact with.

### Hydration mismatches
| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| dates and times formatted differently on server and client (time zones, locales) | format with explicit time zone and locale; render user-local times on the client only |
| random ids or Math.random | {{useId}} for ids |
| browser-only APIs during render (window, localStorage) | read in effects; render a neutral placeholder first |
| user-specific data in cached HTML | don't cache personalised HTML; client-render authenticated parts |
| invalid HTML nesting (div in p) | fix markup |
| browser extensions modifying DOM | suppressHydrationWarning only for specific known cases |

### Banking usage
SSR or static generation for public pages (rates, products, branch finder); authenticated dashboards usually client-rendered or server-rendered without shared caching; never leak one user's data via CDN caches.

  S-->>B: stream balances HTML when its data resolves
  S-->>B: stream transactions HTML later, inside Suspense boundary
  B->>B: load JS, hydrate boundaries as they arrive, user interaction prioritised
  Note over B,S: mismatch if server and client render differently - dates, random ids, window checks

Streaming SSR with Suspense and selective hydration.
Mismatches: dates, random ids, browser APIs, cached personal data.

questions.q: Explain React Server Components and Next.js App Router: what runs where, benefits, and the security pitfalls of server actions.
questions.a:
### Server Components
- Run **only on the server** (at request or build time); can access databases and services directly; their code isn't shipped to the client; output a serialised tree.
- **Client Components** ({{'use client'}}) run on both server (SSR) and client, can use state, effects, browser APIs.
- Props passed from server to client components must be serialisable; server components can render client components and pass server data down.

### Benefits
Smaller bundles (server-only dependencies stay on the server), data fetching close to data sources without client waterfalls, streaming with Suspense, simpler data access for read-heavy pages.

### Server actions ({{'use server'}})
Functions callable from the client that run on the server: forms and mutations without writing API routes.

### Security pitfalls
- Server actions are **public HTTP endpoints**: they must authenticate and authorise every call, validate all inputs (Zod), and never trust hidden form fields.
- Don't pass secrets or excessive data as props to client components (they're serialised to the browser).
- Mark server-only modules ({{import 'server-only'}}) to prevent accidental client import.
- CSRF: frameworks add origin checks; keep them enabled.
- Caching: per-user data must not be statically cached; understand framework caching defaults.

flowchart LR
  subgraph Server
    SC[Server component: fetches data, can read secrets] --> HTML[Serialised RSC payload]
    SA[Server action: validate and authorise every call]
  end
  subgraph Client
    CC[Client component with use client: state, events]
  end
  HTML --> CC
  CC -->|form submit or call| SA
  SC -.->|only serialisable props cross the boundary, never secrets| CC
pts: Server Components run only on the server; no client bundle.
Client Components for interactivity; serialisable props.
Server actions are public endpoints: auth, authz, validation.
Don't serialise secrets or excess data to clients.

### React XSS vectors

- {{dangerouslySetInnerHTML}} with user or CMS content (sanitise with DOMPurify and an allow-list, or render markdown to React elements safely).
- **URLs**: {{href}} or {{src}} with {{javascript:}} schemes from user data (React warns in recent versions but validate schemes yourself).

### CSP
Nonce-based {{script-src}} with {{strict-dynamic}}, no unsafe-inline or unsafe-eval (watch libraries that need eval), strict {{connect-src}}; Trusted Types where possible.

### Third-party code
Minimise scripts on sensitive pages; SRI; npm supply-chain controls; review libraries that touch the DOM.

questions.q: Fetch waterfalls make a dashboard slow. How do you find and eliminate them (parallel queries, loaders, prefetching, BFF aggregation, RSC)?
questions.a:
### What a waterfall is
Component A renders and fetches; only when it finishes does child B render and fetch; then C. Latency adds up: three 300 ms calls become 900 ms plus rendering. Code splitting adds another layer (load chunk, then fetch).

### Finding them
Network panel (staircase pattern), React DevTools showing Suspense boundaries resolving sequentially, RUM timing per widget.

### Fixes
| Technique | How |
|---|---|
| **Hoist and parallelise** | start all independent queries at the route level ({{useQueries}}, loaders, Promise.all) |
| **Route loaders** | fetch in parallel with lazy-loaded code |
| **Prefetching** | on hover or focus of navigation links, prefetch data and code |
| **BFF aggregation** | one request returning what the screen needs (fewer round trips on mobile) |
| **Server Components / server rendering** | fetch close to data sources, stream results |
| **Suspense boundaries** placed so independent sections load in parallel |
| **Dependent queries** only when truly dependent (enabled flag) |

### Caching
Shared query cache prevents refetching the same data in multiple components; staleTime tuned.

questions.q: When are optimistic UI updates appropriate in banking, and how do you implement them with rollback? When must you avoid them?
questions.a:
### Appropriate
Low-risk, reversible, high-confidence actions where the server rarely rejects: renaming an account nickname, toggling notification preferences, marking a message read, reordering favourites.

### Avoid
Money movement outcomes (payments, transfers), limit changes, card freezes where the customer relies on the result for safety, anything regulatory. Show **pending** status until confirmed; if fast, the delay is barely noticeable; if slow, honesty matters more than speed.

### Implementation (TanStack Query)
1. {{onMutate}}: cancel outgoing refetches for affected queries, snapshot previous data, apply optimistic change.
2. {{onError}}: restore the snapshot, show an error.
3. {{onSettled}}: invalidate to sync with server truth.
React 19 {{useOptimistic}} offers a similar pattern within actions.

### Consistency
Optimistic state must be reconciled with server responses (ids assigned by the server, normalised values); concurrent edits from other devices resolved via server versions.

Never for money movement outcomes.

questions.q: A payment flow has edit, review, SCA challenge, submitting, success, failure, timeout and retry states. Why model it as a state machine, and how do you implement it in React?
questions.a:
### Why
Flags-based state ({{isSubmitting}}, {{needsSca}}, {{hasError}}) allows impossible combinations and makes transitions implicit. A **state machine** defines explicit states, allowed events per state, and side effects on transitions: impossible states can't happen, double submissions are ignored by design, and the flow is visualisable for product, risk and QA.

### Options
- {{useReducer}} with a discriminated union (simple machines).
- **XState** (v5) for complex flows: hierarchical and parallel states, delayed transitions (timeouts), invoked services (API calls), visual tooling, and model-based testing.

### Payment flow states
edit, review, scaRequired (awaiting challenge), submitting, succeeded, failed (retryable or not), timedOut (status unknown: poll before allowing retry).

### Key insight for payments
A timeout is **not** a failure: the status is unknown. The machine moves to checking status (poll with the idempotency key) rather than letting the user resubmit.

questions.q: Combine real-time updates (WebSocket or SSE notifications) with TanStack Query. Update the cache or invalidate? How do you handle reconnects?
questions.a:
### Patterns
| Pattern | When |
|---|---|
| **Invalidate on event** | notification says "payment P changed": invalidate related queries; data refetched from the API (single source of truth, simple, safe) |
| **Update cache directly** | event carries complete authoritative data and high frequency makes refetching wasteful (prices); use {{setQueryData}} with version checks |
| Hybrid | patch status immediately, invalidate details lazily |

### Banking default
Invalidate for business entities (payments, balances): events are hints; the API returns authoritative data with authorisation applied. Direct updates for market data streams.

### Reconnects
- Events missed during disconnects: on reconnect, **invalidate** affected queries (or fetch changes since a cursor).
- Exponential backoff with jitter; pause when the tab is hidden; one connection per app (shared).
- Order: use versions or timestamps to ignore stale events.

### Security
Authenticate the connection (cookie via BFF), authorise subscriptions server-side, never trust event payloads for sensitive decisions.

### Vite

questions.q: Modernise a large legacy React codebase (class components, Redux with connect, React 16/17) to React 19 with hooks. How do you plan it?

### Upgrade path
1. Upgrade React step by step (17 to 18: createRoot, automatic batching, StrictMode effects double-invoke; 18 to 19: removed legacy APIs such as string refs, legacy context, propTypes and defaultProps on function components, ReactDOM.render).
2. Run official **codemods** for API changes; fix StrictMode warnings first on 18.3 (warns about removed APIs).
3. Update ecosystem libraries (router, state, testing) to compatible versions.

### Modernisation
- Class components stay working: convert opportunistically when touched, or prioritise components blocking new patterns (error-prone lifecycle logic).
- Redux: adopt Redux Toolkit; move server data to TanStack Query or RTK Query; replace connect with hooks.
- Remove effects that sync derived state while converting.
- Enable the React Compiler for components following the rules (lint plugin first).

### Process
Small PRs, feature flags for risky changes, tests (Testing Library) added before refactors of critical flows, scorecard per package, lint rules preventing legacy patterns in new code.

| Hosting | CDN + existing .NET services | Node runtime (containers or managed platforms) |

| Option | Notes |

Version alignment of React and shared libraries, duplicate dependencies, cross-app state and routing, consistent UX, testing the composed product, performance overhead, operational complexity (many deployments to coordinate).

Monorepo with domain packages and enforced boundaries, trunk-based development and continuous deployment: most teams get independence in code ownership without runtime integration complexity.

questions.q: Should the bank share code between its React web app and a React Native mobile app? What can be shared, and what shouldn't be?

### Shareable
| Layer | Shareable? |
|---|---|
| domain logic (validation rules, formatting, calculations) | yes: pure TypeScript packages |

| server-state hooks (TanStack Query) | yes (works in both) |
| state machines (XState) for flows | yes |

| UI components | partially: React Native Web or universal libraries (Tamagui, Expo Router web) |
| navigation, platform APIs (biometrics, secure storage, push) | no: platform-specific |

- Universal UI reduces duplication but can compromise native feel or web accessibility; banking apps often prefer native-quality UI per platform with shared logic.

- Release cadence differs (app stores vs continuous web deploys): shared packages need versioning discipline.

### Recommendation
Share domain logic, API layer, state machines and tokens via a monorepo; keep UI and platform integrations platform-specific unless the product is a simple app where universal UI suffices.

questions.q: Design the authentication and API access architecture for React banking apps (web and partner portals): BFF, token handling, CSRF, session management and step-up.
questions.a:
### Architecture
- **BFF per app** (ASP.NET Core with Duende BFF or YARP): OIDC confidential client; tokens stored server-side; browser gets an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie ({{__Host-}} prefix).
- React calls same-origin BFF endpoints; BFF proxies to APIs with access tokens (and token exchange for downstream audiences).
- **CSRF**: SameSite plus a required custom header ({{X-CSRF}}) on all BFF API calls.
- **Session management**: idle and absolute timeouts; warning dialog with extension; back-channel logout from the IdP; logout clears client caches.
- **Step-up**: BFF returns a structured 401 challenge; React redirects through the BFF login endpoint with acr_values and returns to the same screen with preserved state.
- **Real-time**: SignalR or SSE through the BFF with the same cookie.

### Benefits
No tokens in JavaScript (XSS can't steal them), consistent security reviews, central place for headers, rate limits and audit.

### Costs
BFF availability and scaling; same-site deployment requirements; added hop.

| code | lint rules enforced (react-hooks, react-compiler), effect cleanup reviews, derive instead of sync state |
| testing | soak test: Playwright script navigating repeatedly for an hour, tracking JS heap ({{performance.memory}} in Chromium) |
| release | canary for staff apps, quick rollback |
| monitoring | RUM for long tasks, crash or reload rates, memory sampling in Chromium-based environments |

questions.q: Use feature flags and experimentation in React banking apps responsibly: delivery, targeting, performance, security and cleanup.
questions.a:
### Uses
Decouple deploy from release, progressive rollouts (staff, then 5% of customers), kill switches for risky features, A/B tests on non-regulated UX (copy, layout), entitlement-based features.

### Implementation
- Flags evaluated **server-side** (BFF) for anything security-relevant; the client receives evaluated flags for UX only (never trust client flags to gate access).
- OpenFeature React SDK or a vendor SDK; flags loaded with the session to avoid flicker; defaults safe if the flag service fails.

### Experimentation in banking
Regulated communications (fees, risk warnings, consumer duty) can't be A/B tested freely: involve compliance; measure outcomes, not just clicks (good customer outcomes).

### Performance
Avoid layout shifts from late flag evaluation (bootstrap flags), avoid bundling both variants of heavy features (lazy-load the variant).

### Cleanup
Flags have owners and expiry; lint or CI warnings for expired flags; remove code paths after rollout.

questions.q: What do React 19.2's Activity component and useEffectEvent solve, and how do they change the way you write tabbed UIs and effects?
questions.a:
### Activity
{{<Activity mode="visible" | "hidden">}} keeps a subtree **mounted but hidden**. In hidden mode React unmounts the subtree's effects (subscriptions stop, timers clear), hides it from the DOM, and renders updates to it at low priority. Switching back to visible restores the previous state (form input, scroll position, local state) instantly, without re-fetching or re-mounting.

| Approach | State kept? | Effects running while hidden? | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| conditional render ({{cond && <Tab/>}}) | no, lost on hide | no | re-mount and re-fetch on show |
| CSS display none | yes | yes, subscriptions keep running | wasted work, stale side effects |
| {{<Activity mode="hidden">}} | yes | no, effects cleaned up and re-created on show | memory for the hidden tree |

Good uses: tabbed account views, a payment wizard where users go back a step, pre-rendering the next likely screen in the background.

### useEffectEvent
Effects often need the **latest** value of something (theme, user preferences, a callback prop) without re-running when it changes. Adding it to the dependency array reconnects the effect (for example, a WebSocket) every time; leaving it out gives a stale closure and a lint warning. {{useEffectEvent}} creates a function that always sees the latest props and state but is not a dependency, so the effect re-runs only for what really defines it.

Rules: call effect events only from inside effects (not during render, not passed to children); keep the real dependencies (the connection's account id) in the array.
pts: Activity hides a subtree but keeps its state.
Hidden mode cleans up effects; visible restores them.
useEffectEvent reads latest values without being a dependency.

questions.q: React 19 lets components render title, meta and link tags and call preload APIs. How do document metadata and resource hints work, and how do you use them for performance?
questions.a:
### Document metadata in components
React 19 hoists {{<title>}}, {{<meta>}} and {{<link>}} rendered anywhere in the tree into the document head, on the client and in server rendering. A route component can declare its own title and canonical link without a helmet library. Frameworks with their own metadata API (Next.js {{metadata}} exports) still take precedence for their routes.

### Stylesheets with precedence
{{<link rel="stylesheet" href="..." precedence="default">}} tells React to insert the stylesheet once, in precedence order, and to **suspend** the boundary until it has loaded, which avoids flashes of unstyled content when a lazily loaded component brings its own CSS.

### Resource hint APIs (react-dom)
| API | Effect | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| {{prefetchDNS(href)}} | DNS lookup early | third-party origins used later |
| {{preconnect(href)}} | DNS, TCP and TLS early | API and CDN origins needed soon |
| {{preload(href, { as })}} | download a resource with high priority | LCP image, critical font |
| {{preloadModule(href)}} | download an ES module | the next route's chunk |
| {{preinit(href, { as })}} | download and execute or apply | a script or stylesheet needed immediately |

Called during render (or in an event handler), these deduplicate automatically and, in SSR, are emitted early in the streamed HTML.

### Guidance
Preload only what the current view needs to paint; over-preloading pushes the LCP resource down the queue. Preconnect to at most a few origins. Measure with field LCP, not just Lighthouse.
pts: title, meta and link are hoisted to the head.
Stylesheets with precedence load once and suspend until ready.

questions.q: How do you animate route and state changes in React with the View Transitions API and React's ViewTransition component, and what are the caveats?
questions.a:
### The browser API
{{document.startViewTransition(update)}} snapshots the current page, runs the DOM update, then animates from the old snapshot to the new one with CSS ({{::view-transition-old}}, {{::view-transition-new}}). Elements with the same {{view-transition-name}} animate between positions, giving shared-element transitions with no JavaScript animation library.

### React's ViewTransition component
React's {{<ViewTransition>}} (experimental; available in the experimental and canary channels at the time of writing) integrates this with React's scheduling: when an update runs inside {{startTransition}} or a Suspense reveal, React starts a view transition and applies names to the wrapped elements automatically. It answers when an animation runs (enter, exit, update, shared element) and which CSS class is applied.

### Without the experimental component
Call {{document.startViewTransition}} yourself around a {{flushSync}} state update, or use the router's built-in support where it exists. Feature-detect and fall back to an instant update.

### Caveats
- Transitions block interaction briefly while the snapshot animates; keep them under about 300 ms.
- Honour {{prefers-reduced-motion}}.
- Names must be unique on the page at the moment of the snapshot; duplicates cancel the transition.
- Do not animate critical financial information in a way that could mislead (a balance sliding into place from another account).
pts: Browser snapshots old and new DOM and animates between them.
Shared elements via matching view-transition-name.
React's ViewTransition component is experimental; plain API works today.

questions.q: Explain caching and revalidation in the Next.js App Router (fetch cache, "use cache", tags, revalidatePath, partial prerendering). How do you keep financial data fresh while pages stay fast?
questions.a:
### Layers of caching in the App Router
| Layer | What is cached | Controlled by |
|---|---|---|
| request memoisation | identical fetch calls within one render | automatic, per request |
| data cache | results of fetch or cached functions across requests | fetch options, the "use cache" directive with a cache lifetime |
| full route cache | rendered HTML and RSC payload for static routes | static versus dynamic rendering |
| router cache (client) | RSC payloads for visited and prefetched routes | navigation, router.refresh |

### Cache components and "use cache"
Recent Next.js versions (Cache Components, Next.js 16) make caching **opt-in**: a function, component or file marked {{"use cache"}} is cached with a lifetime ({{cacheLife}}) and tags ({{cacheTag}}); everything else renders dynamically per request. **Partial prerendering** serves a static shell immediately and streams the dynamic holes inside Suspense boundaries.

### Invalidation
- {{revalidateTag(tag)}} or {{updateTag(tag)}} after a mutation (in a server action) invalidates every cached entry with that tag.
- {{revalidatePath(path)}} invalidates a route.
- Time-based lifetimes for data that can be slightly stale.

### Financial data rules
| Data | Strategy |
|---|---|
| product rates, fee schedules (public) | cached with tags; revalidated when the rates service publishes a change; show "rates as at" time |
| account balances, transactions | never shared-cached; render dynamically per user, private, inside Suspense |
| reference data (currencies, BIC lists) | long lifetime, tagged |
| anything after a user's own payment | server action updates, then revalidates the user's tag so the next view is fresh |

Never put per-user data in a cache keyed without the user, and check that a dynamic API (cookies, headers) is not hidden inside a cached function.

questions.q: What is the React Native New Architecture (JSI, Fabric, TurboModules, bridgeless), and what does it mean for a bank deciding on a mobile stack?
questions.a:
### Old versus new
The old architecture sent JSON messages over an asynchronous **bridge** between JavaScript and native code: slow for large data, no synchronous calls, and layout jank under load. The New Architecture (default since React Native 0.76):
| Piece | What it does |
|---|---|
| **JSI** (JavaScript Interface) | JavaScript holds direct references to C++ host objects; calls are synchronous where needed, no serialisation |
| **Fabric** | new renderer with a C++ core; supports concurrent React features (transitions, Suspense) and consistent layout |
| **TurboModules** | native modules loaded lazily and called through JSI with typed interfaces generated by **Codegen** |
| **Bridgeless mode** | removes the bridge entirely |
| **Hermes** | the default JavaScript engine: bytecode precompiled at build time, faster start-up, lower memory |

### Implications for a bank
- **Performance**: smoother lists and faster start-up make React Native credible for mainstream banking apps; heavy work (crypto, image processing) still belongs in native modules.
- **Libraries**: check that every dependency supports the New Architecture; unmaintained native modules are the main migration blocker.
- **Security**: secure storage (Keychain, Keystore), certificate pinning, jailbreak and root detection, and app attestation (App Attest, Play Integrity) are native concerns accessed via modules; review them like any security component.
- **Code sharing with web**: share types, API clients, validation and state logic; UI usually differs (React Native primitives versus DOM), though React Native Web or a universal framework (Expo Router) can share some screens.
- **Team**: React and TypeScript skills transfer; you still need iOS and Android engineers for native modules, releases and store compliance.

### Decision factors
Existing native teams and apps, need for platform-specific UX, performance-critical features, release cadence (over-the-air updates for JavaScript changes within store rules), and long-term framework stability.

questions.q: React Server Components and Server Actions moved code to the server. What is the security model, what went wrong in the December 2025 RSC vulnerability, and how do you govern RSC apps?
questions.a:
### The model
- Server Components run only on the server; their output is serialised into the **RSC payload** (the "Flight" format) streamed to the browser.
- Anything passed as a prop to a Client Component is serialised and sent to the browser. Secrets must never cross that boundary.
- **Server Actions** are compiled into HTTP endpoints with generated ids. Any client can call them with any arguments; they are public APIs, whatever the UI suggests.

### The December 2025 vulnerability
In early December 2025 a critical remote code execution flaw (CVE-2025-55182) was disclosed in the React Server Components packages: crafted requests to server-function endpoints could abuse how the server **deserialised** the Flight payload and execute code. It affected React 19 RSC implementations and frameworks built on them (including Next.js App Router) until patched releases shipped; exploitation started within days. Lessons:
- The RSC wire protocol is attack surface, like any deserialiser.
- Framework and React versions are now security-critical dependencies: you need the ability to patch and redeploy within hours.
- WAF rules can buy time, but patching is the fix.

### Controls
| Risk | Control |
|---|---|
| secrets leaking into props | server-only modules ({{import 'server-only'}}), taint APIs, data transfer objects for client props |
| unauthorised server actions | authenticate and authorise inside every action; validate input with a schema |
| CSRF on actions | same-origin checks are built in; keep cookies SameSite; do not disable origin checks |
| IDOR | check ownership of every id received |
| deserialisation and framework bugs | dependency monitoring, fast patch pipeline, WAF virtual patching |
| over-fetching | DTOs, not ORM entities, as props |

cheat:
### Model
UI = f(state): render (pure, may be repeated or discarded) then commit. Renders triggered by state, parent renders, context, external stores. Reconciliation by type and position; keys for lists (stable ids; change key to reset state); Fiber enables interruptible, prioritised rendering. Never define components inside components.

### Hooks
useState (batched, functional updates), useReducer with discriminated unions for complex flows, rules of hooks. useEffect only for external systems: cleanup, dependencies, abort fetches; derive state during render, reset with keys, handle events in handlers. Refs for DOM and mutable values; React 19 ref as prop, ref callback cleanup, use(), actions (useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic). Custom hooks expose domain APIs.

### Performance
memo, useMemo, useCallback only where profiling shows value; React Compiler auto-memoises code following the Rules of React. State colocation; split contexts; stores with selectors (useSyncExternalStore prevents tearing). Transitions and useDeferredValue for responsiveness; virtualisation; workers; rAF batching for real-time grids. Route-level lazy loading, loaders, prefetching, BFF aggregation; budgets and RUM with attribution.

### Data and state
Server state in TanStack Query (key factories, staleTime, invalidation after mutations, clear on logout). URL state in search params. Forms with React Hook Form + Zod; server validation authoritative; idempotent submits; no optimistic money movement. Client state local first, Zustand or Redux Toolkit when shared. State machines for payment flows (timeout means unknown status).

### Rendering modes
SSR and hydration (useId, explicit formatting, no browser APIs in render), streaming with Suspense, RSC and server actions (public endpoints: authenticate, authorise, validate; don't serialise secrets). SPA + .NET BFF for authenticated apps; frameworks for SEO-heavy public sites.

### Quality
Error boundaries per widget and route, root error callbacks, chunk failure handling, telemetry with release and trace context. Security: no dangerouslySetInnerHTML without sanitiser, safe href schemes, no spreading untrusted props, BFF cookies, CSP and Trusted Types. Accessibility with semantics and headless primitives, focus management, live regions, axe. Testing Library + MSW, Playwright on multiple engines, contract checks.

### Principal moves
Explicit standards for the React stack via templates and lint rules; modular monolith before micro-frontends; share logic, not UI, with React Native; domain-owned hooks and query keys; performance programme with ownership; BFF-based auth with step-up; soak tests and canaries; CRA to Vite migration; server-evaluated feature flags; AI UIs with safe rendering and confirmable actions.

### Added diagrams to remember
- Render phase is pure and interruptible; commit is synchronous; layout effects before paint, effects after.
- Effect race: cleanup sets an ignore flag or aborts the request, so a late response cannot overwrite newer state.
- TanStack Query: fresh = cached, stale = cached plus background refetch, mutations invalidate keys.
- One error boundary plus Suspense per independent widget.
- Transitions: urgent input commits now, the expensive render restarts with the latest value.
- RSC boundary: only serialisable props cross to the client; every server action authorises itself.
